lens: Adversarial arithmetic and statistical audit: split-adjustment maths recomputed by brute force against real corporate actions, return compounding and benchmark-excess windows re-derived, the deflated Sharpe implementation compared numerically against Bailey & Lopez de Prado, and every summary statistic re-run to check its denominator and its effective sample size. Three numbers recomputed by hand (TRENT 2016 split, CUPID 2024 double action, the 42.6% random baseline) and the look-ahead detector executed against a deliberately leaky filings strategy.

findings.problem: The deflated Sharpe is not Bailey & Lopez de Prado's formula. Three separate defects. (a) It CRASHES for n_trials of 1 or 2: max(N,2)/2.71828 = 0.7358, ln of that is negative, sqrt raises ValueError. The guard `if n_trials < 1` does not protect. (b) It omits sqrt(V), the cross-trial variance of the Sharpe estimates, hardcoding V=1. In the paper E[max SR] = sqrt(V)*[(1-g)Z^-1(1-1/N) + g*Z^-1(1-1/(Ne))]; the code drops sqrt(V) entirely. (c) It replaces the two inverse-normal quantiles with the crude asymptotic sqrt(2 ln N), which overstates the paper's E[max] by 9-17%. Combined, the function is a step function at e_max, not a probability.
findings.evidence:
deflated_sharpe(0.06, n_trials=1, 2500) RAISES ValueError: expected a nonnegative input, got -0.6137042935746733  (same for n_trials=2)

N=20: code e_max=2.1881, Bailey/LdP e_max=1.9007 (+15.1%). N=5: 1.3958 vs 1.1926 (+17.0%). N=1000: 3.5556 vs 3.2551 (+9.2%).

Output is binary, with essentially no sensitivity to sample size:
  SR=0.05 n=20 T=2500 -> 0.000000
  SR=0.50 n=20 T=2500 -> 0.000000
  SR=2.00 n=20 T=2500 -> 0.000000
  SR=3.00 n=20 T=2500 -> 1.000000
  T=12 monthly obs, 20 trials, Sharpe 3.0 -> 0.8746
findings.why_it_inflates: This is the project's designated anti-overfitting gate, and its docstring sets the bar at 0.95. Because sqrt(T-1) is ~50 for daily data while e_max is stuck at ~2.2, the function returns 0.00 for every realistic input and flips to 1.00 the instant the Sharpe crosses ~2.2. The docstring itself talks about 'a Sharpe of 1.5', i.e. an ANNUALISED figure, so the natural call site passes an annualised Sharpe with n_obs = number of days. Any annualised Sharpe above ~2.2 then returns 1.0000 — certainty that the result is real — no matter how many variants were tried or how few observations exist. It will rubber-stamp precisely the overfit, high-Sharpe backtest it exists to reject, and it will do so with the paper's authority attached. Twelve monthly observations and a Sharpe of 3.0 already scores 0.87.
findings.fix: Replace e_max with the paper's expression using statistics.NormalDist().inv_cdf: sr0 = sqrt(V)*((1-g)*Z(1-1/N) + g*Z(1-1/(N*e))), return 0.0 (not a crash) for N==1 so DSR degenerates to the plain PSR, and require the caller to pass V, the variance of the Sharpe estimates across the logged trials (computable from state/trials.jsonl). Assert in the signature that observed_sharpe and n_obs share a frequency — take per-period Sharpe and periods, or take annualised Sharpe plus periods_per_year and convert internally. Add a unit test pinning DSR against a worked example from the paper, and a test that n_trials=1 returns the PSR rather than raising.

findings.problem: The look-ahead detector physically truncates ONLY the prices table. `_truncated_copy` calls `out.execute(store.SCHEMA)`, and store.SCHEMA creates exactly one table. announcements, financials, indices and corpactions do not exist in the truncated database at all, so a strategy that reads any of them raises CatalogException instead of being tested. `stability()` passes raise_on_fail=False, which suppresses LeakDetected only — a CatalogException still kills the whole run.
findings.evidence:
tables in truncated copy: ['prices']

Ran future_blindness against a strategy that reads announcements with NO asof filter whatsoever (an open, deliberate leak):
  future_blindness on an OPENLY LEAKY filings strategy -> CatalogException : Catalog Error: Table with name announcements does not exist!

It did not report a leak. It could not run at all.
findings.why_it_inflates: This is the single control the whole repository is built around — the module docstring says 'This is the test that a one-day shift error fails immediately.' It cannot be run on any strategy that touches filings or fundamentals, which is exactly what jobs/study_filings.py and the intended strategy use. The announcement archive is the one place where a one-day shift can hide (an_dt vs trade_date), and it is the only table the detector cannot see. A filings strategy will therefore ship with zero look-ahead evidence while the repository's own documentation implies it was cleared. That is the same shape of unearned confidence that produced the fictitious 30% CAGR.
findings.fix: Truncate every point-in-time table, each on its own time key: prices/indices/corpactions on date <= asof, announcements on an_dt < the asof session open (not trade_date — an_dt is the boundary), financials on the filing/publication timestamp, not the period end. Build the schema by copying the source connection's table definitions rather than importing store.SCHEMA. Add a test alongside tests/test_leak.py containing a Leaky strategy that cheats via announcements, and assert it raises LeakDetected — a detector that has never been shown to fail on a filings leak proves nothing about filings.

findings.problem: When a symbol has two adjustable actions on the SAME ex-date (a split and a bonus on the same day is routine in India), merge_asof matches only one of the two rows and applies only that row's cumulative factor. The other action is silently dropped from the back-adjustment. Brute-force recomputation of the correct factor (product of every factor with ex_date > price date) disagrees with what adjusted_prices produces for 17 of the 33 affected symbols.
findings.evidence:
Recomputed the truth for every price row of the 33 symbols that have same-day double actions:
MISMATCHED symbols: 17
  ('CUPID',      1352 rows wrong of 2463, truth=0.0100, applied=0.1000, from 2018-10-11)
  ('VAISHALI',   1174 of 1643, truth=0.1000,  applied=0.5000)
  ('AHCL',        156 of  250, truth=0.1000,  applied=0.5000)
  ('BESTAGRO',   1038 of 1196, truth=0.0667,  applied=0.6667)
  ('DELPHIFX',   1100 of 1239, truth=0.0667,  applied=0.2000)
  ('BHARATRAS',  2703 of 2884, truth=0.2500,  applied=0.5000)
  ...17 in total

CUPID has Bonus 1:1 (0.5) AND a 10:1 split (0.1) both on 2024-04-04. The harness applies 0.1 where 0.05 is required, so every pre-2024 entry price is exactly 10x too high.
findings.why_it_inflates: The applied factor is always LARGER than the truth, so a window that opens before the double action and closes after it computes an entry price 2x to 10x too high and reports a return that is 50% to 90% too low. That is not noise: companies do split-plus-bonus after a large rise, so the error lands on the exact names a screen is supposed to find, and it lands only on them. It also runs the other way for any window that opens after the action, so the same symbol contributes both a fabricated disaster and a clean number to the same distribution. Every median, mean, worst_pct and multibagger_pct in every study is contaminated, and the sign of the contamination is not uniform across the sample.
findings.fix: Collapse corpactions to one row per (symbol, ex_date) before computing the cumulative product — group by symbol and ex_date and take prod(factor) — then run the reverse cumprod on the collapsed frame. Add a regression test that asserts adjusted_prices matches a brute-force product-of-factors-after-date for every symbol with more than one action, not just the double-action ones.

findings.line_hint: _SPLIT regex line ~62, _BONUS regex line ~70, parse_factor lines 73-105
findings.problem: The _SPLIT regex demands the literal 'per share' between the two face values, and _BONUS demands whitespace immediately after the word 'bonus'. NSE's own subject strings do not always oblige. Sixteen genuine equity splits and bonuses parse to factor NULL and are therefore never adjusted at all. parse_factor returns ('split', None) and the row is stored, so nothing downstream flags it — the action is visible in the table but invisible to the adjustment.
findings.evidence:
16 real actions with factor NULL (excluding the bonus-debenture and bonus-NCRPS rows, which correctly should not adjust):
  TRENT 2016-09-12 'Face Value Split From Rs 10 To Re 1'      <- no 'Per Share'
  GRASIM 2016-10-06 'Face Value Split From Rs 10 To Re 2'
  VGUARD, KAJARIACER, UNOMINDA, LUXIND, PNCINFRA, AEGISLOG, GRANULES, SHAH,
  JMTAUTOLTD, LAMBODHARA, SARLAPOLY, CORPBANK ('Face Valus Split' - NSE typo),
  MOTHERSON 2015-07-23 '... / Bonus - 1:2'                    <- hyphen, not space
  AJANTPHARM 2022-06-22 'Bonus- 1:2'                          <- hyphen, not space

Hand-recomputed TRENT:
  2016-09-09 close 2344.80 ; 2016-09-12 close 241.45
  as the harness measures it : -89.7%
  truth (2344.80 x 0.1 = 234.48) : +3.0%
  error injected into any window spanning this date: -92.7 pts
findings.why_it_inflates: A single -89.7% fabricated day sits inside every 3/6/12/24-month window that straddles 2016-09-12 for TRENT, one of the decade's largest multibaggers. It destroys median_stock_pct, drives worst_pct to a fictitious number, and zeroes the multibagger count for the affected names. The published study asserts the numbers are 'split-adjusted'; for these sixteen names that claim is false, and the reader has no way to see it because the actions are present in the corpactions table. The direction is deflating for these names, which is worse than it sounds: it makes a signal that happens to select splitting companies look broken, and it will be read as evidence against a real effect.
findings.fix: Make 'per share' optional and allow hyphens: r"from\s+rs?e?\.?\s*(\d+(?:\.\d+)?)\s*/?-?\s*(?:per\s+share\s+)?to\s+rs?e?\.?\s*(\d+(?:\.\d+)?)" and r"bonus\s*[-:]?\s*(\d+)\s*:\s*(\d+)", keeping the existing exclusion of debenture/NCRPS bonuses. Then add the control that matters more than the regex: a job that flags every date where a symbol's adjusted close moves more than 35% in one session with no adjustable action on file, and fails loudly. That catches the next unparsed format instead of waiting for someone to notice.

findings.problem: The momentum strategy ranks on RAW closes. _panel selects `close` straight from prices and never calls eventstudy.adjusted_prices or corpactions.adjust_prices. Any name that split or issued a bonus inside the 252-session formation window has its formation return understated by a factor of 1/factor, i.e. 2x to 10x, and is pushed to the bottom of the ranking.
findings.evidence:
93 symbols have a split or bonus inside the current 12-1 formation window (2025-08-01 to 2026-08-06). Worked examples, raw vs true formation return:
  TFCILTD    factor 0.2 : raw -60.0%  true  +99.9%
  ADANIPOWER factor 0.2 : raw -64.1%  true  +79.6%
  ZYDUSWELL  factor 0.2 : raw -73.2%  true  +34.0%
  STEELCAS   factor 0.2 : raw -67.6%  true  +62.2%
All four are genuine 12-month winners recorded as heavy losers.
findings.why_it_inflates: Momentum exists here purely as a calibration instrument — the docstring says 'If our validation says this earns 40% a year, the harness is broken.' The test is one-sided: it only alarms on a result that is too good. A ranking that has silently ejected its true winners will return a weak, unremarkable number, that number will pass the calibration, and the harness will be declared trustworthy on the strength of a signal that was never actually computed. Every subsequent study inherits that unearned clearance. The one check designed to prove the machinery works is currently incapable of failing.
findings.fix: Route _panel through the same adjusted-price path the event study uses, so formation returns, the min_price filter and the liquidity median all run on adjusted numbers. Then make the calibration two-sided: assert the measured 12-1 spread falls inside a stated plausible band for Indian equities (roughly 3-12% a year gross of costs), and fail the harness when the answer is implausibly LOW as well as implausibly high.

findings.problem: summarise() reports point estimates with no uncertainty of any kind, and its denominator (`scored`) is a count of EVENTS, not of independent observations. The random baseline's 2,220 scored twelve-month rows come from only 37 distinct dates, 60 correlated picks per date, all sharing the same market window. The naive binomial standard error understates the true one by a factor of two, and nothing in the output reveals the date count.
findings.evidence:
Reproduced the published baseline exactly:
  h=12m: beat_bmk=42.6%  n_obs=2220 over only 37 dates
  naive SE = 1.05 pts   date-clustered SE = 2.07 pts  (2.0x larger)
  per-date hit rate range: 18% to 67%
  95% CI (clustered): 38.5% to 46.6%

And the point estimate itself is unstable:
  seed=7 -> 42.6% | seed=11 -> 41.4% | seed=23 -> 42.7% | seed=101 -> 41.1%
  baseline_dates=40 -> 42.6% | 50 -> 41.7% (the date grid is dates[::step][:n], so changing n changes the whole grid)

The published volume results (39.0%, 40.4%, 40.8%, 42.5%) all sit inside the baseline's own 38.5-46.6% interval.
findings.why_it_inflates: research/studies/volume_anomaly.md states as established fact that volume spikes 'beat the benchmark LESS often than stocks picked at random' and reports a 42.6% vs 39-41% gap. That gap is smaller than the baseline's clustered standard error and smaller than the swing produced by changing the random seed. The same applies to the multibagger claim (11.5% vs 9.1%) which rests on far fewer effective observations. This finding is now carried forward as a settled prior that must not be re-tested — a false negative frozen into the project's assumptions, which is the most expensive kind, because nothing will ever revisit it. The identical machinery will report the filings study, where a spurious positive would be acted on with real capital.
findings.fix: Add to summarise(): n_dates, n_symbols, and a date-clustered standard error and 95% CI for every rate (block bootstrap resampling whole signal dates, not individual events). Refuse to print a rate when n_dates is below ~100. Make baseline() sample the SAME dates the events occur on, weighted by event count per date, so the comparison is date-matched, and pass the variant's own min_turnover_cr into baseline() — the 5cr variant is currently compared against a 1cr baseline. Restate the volume study's conclusion as 'no detectable effect, and the sample cannot resolve a gap of this size' rather than 'slightly negative'.

findings.problem: find_events computes vol_ratio from raw volume and day_return from raw close/prev_close. NSE's bhavcopy prev_close is NOT adjusted for splits or bonuses, and share counts jump mechanically on the ex-date, so both quantities are corrupted on every one of the 856 adjustable ex-dates. The eventstudy adjusts prices; the signal that selects the events does not.
findings.evidence:
Verified prev_close on ex-dates is unadjusted — every single one shows the mechanical fall:
  2026-08-25 CORDELIA  prev_close 1043.60 close 104.45  factor 0.10  day_ret -90.0%
  2026-06-24 KOTYARK   prev_close  453.80 close  43.30  factor 0.0909 day_ret -90.5%
  2026-08-21 GOODLUCK  prev_close 1439.40 close 490.90  factor 0.333  day_ret -65.9%

In the vol_x=5 event set (222,914 events): 339 events fall exactly on a split/bonus ex-date, median day_return -78.8%. Volume ratios are mechanically inflated too:
  2026-01-16 BESTAGRO vol_ratio 333.8, day_return -93.2% (10:1 split + 1:2 bonus)
  2023-02-24 VINNY    vol_ratio  26.6, day_return -95.4%
  2024-04-04 CUPID    vol_ratio  23.2, day_return -94.8%
findings.why_it_inflates: Splits inject guaranteed events: the share count multiplies, so the volume ratio clears any threshold by construction, and companies split after a rally. The 'volume 5x + price up' variant additionally uses `close > prev_close` as its filter, which on an ex-date is a comparison against a stale pre-split reference — that variant's membership is decided partly by a number that means nothing. So the signal set is contaminated with mechanical, non-informative events that are systematically drawn from post-rally names, and the study's central inversion (P(outcome | signal)) is being computed over a signal that is partly an accounting artefact rather than an observation about trading interest.
findings.fix: Build find_events on the adjusted panel: derive prev_close as the lag of adjusted close within the symbol rather than trusting the bhavcopy field, and divide volume by the corpaction factor (shares multiply by 1/factor) before computing the ratio. As a floor, exclude any session within 5 trading days of an adjustable ex-date from the event set and report how many events that removes.

findings.line_hint: measure, entry_px at line ~172, bm_entry at line ~186, bm_ret at lines ~217-222
findings.problem: The stock leg is measured from the entry day's adjusted OPEN; the benchmark leg is measured from the entry day's CLOSE. The two windows therefore differ by one intraday session at the entry end, and the module docstring's claim that 'the index return is measured over the identical calendar window as the stock, from the same entry date' is not true. The indices table carries an open column, so the correct value is available and unused.
findings.evidence:
Entry-day open-to-close move on the day the study buys, over the 222,725 vol_x=5 entries:
  median -0.793%   mean -0.565%
Against the unconditional figure for all stock-days 2016-2026:
  median -0.362%   mean -0.304%
So the volume-spike entries carry roughly 0.43 pt of extra intraday drift that is charged to the stock leg and never to the index leg.
(The exit end is correctly aligned — I checked it separately: only 2 of 1,926 twelve-month rows had a stock exit date later than the benchmark exit date.)
findings.why_it_inflates: The sign depends entirely on the signal. For a volume spike it deflates by ~0.8 pt. For a positive-news signal — an order win or a guidance upgrade, exactly what jobs/study_filings.py tests — the day-after-the-filing open-to-close drift is typically positive, and that drift is handed to the stock while the benchmark is denied it. A systematic 0.5-1.0 pt tilt is decisive in a study whose entire published conclusion turns on a 1.8 pt gap between 40.8% and 42.6%.
findings.fix: Take bm_entry from the benchmark's OPEN on entry_date (indices.open exists) so both legs start at the same moment, and keep both exits on the close. If a benchmark open is missing for a date, mark that event unscored rather than falling back to the close.

findings.line_hint: measure, delisted flag line ~181 and the elif delisted branch at lines ~200-206
findings.problem: Two problems in one branch. First, `delisted` is a SYMBOL-level flag (sym_last < last_session - 30d) applied to every event for that symbol regardless of the event's own date. Second, when the branch fires the STOCK window is truncated to the last traded price but the BENCHMARK window is still measured to `target` = entry + h months, and when target runs past the index data it silently falls back to bm.iloc[-1]. The two legs then cover different periods, and the row is nonetheless labelled complete=True and counted in every statistic. Symbol renames — routine on NSE — are indistinguishable from delistings here and get the same treatment.
findings.evidence:
On the 2,400-event random baseline, 12.2% of rows carry the delisted flag at every horizon (294 of 2,400). Rows counted as complete 24-month outcomes while actually held under 600 days: 81 of 1,989. Their leg mismatch:
  h=24m delisted: median stock_ret -6.1%, median bmk_ret +26.5%, median excess -33.5%
The -33.5% median excess is a stock return over a truncated life differenced against a benchmark return over the full two years.
findings.why_it_inflates: Every one of those rows is a difference of two returns measured over different lengths of time, presented as an excess return. The study writeup leans on this directly — 'Between 294 and 392 names in each sample delisted... dropping them would have lifted every number in this table' — which reads as a careful anti-survivorship choice, but the magnitude of that claimed effect is itself manufactured by the window mismatch rather than measured. Because the flag is symbol-level, a company that merely changed ticker has its entire history relabelled as a terminal outcome. And complete=True on these rows makes a thin 24-month sample look adequately powered, defeating the module's own stated protection against exactly that.
findings.fix: Decide delisting per event, not per symbol: an event is truncated only when the symbol's last session falls inside that event's own horizon. When truncating the stock leg, truncate the benchmark leg to the SAME exit date. Add a third state alongside complete/incomplete — 'truncated' — carrying the actual holding days, report its count separately in summarise(), and never let a truncated row silently join a full-horizon distribution. Cross-check the flagged symbols against corpactions and the NSE symbol-change list so renames are excluded before anything is called a delisting.

findings.problem: _trade_date rolls after-hours filings forward by one calendar day and then rolls weekends to Monday, but it has no notion of the NSE trading calendar. A filing made after 15:30 on the evening before a market holiday is stamped with a date on which no session exists. study_filings.py then joins `p.date = a.trade_date`, so those events are silently dropped rather than rolled to the next real session.
findings.evidence: Announcement (trade_date, symbol) pairs landing on a date that has no row in prices: 14,780 of 275,915 (5.4%).
findings.why_it_inflates: It does not create a leak — the direction is conservative — but it removes 5.4% of the filing archive from every study non-randomly. Indian market holidays cluster around Diwali, Holi and the results-heavy periods that follow long weekends, so the dropped filings are concentrated in specific weeks rather than spread evenly. The filing study's event counts and hit rates are computed over a sample with a calendar-shaped hole in it, and nothing in the output reports the loss.
findings.fix: Roll trade_date forward to the next date that actually appears in the prices archive rather than to the next weekday, and log the count of filings that had to be rolled more than one session. Separately, tighten the after-hours boundary: the current test (hour >= 16, or hour == 15 and minute > 30) leaves 15:30:01 through 15:30:59 attributed to the same session.

findings.line_hint: _at_or_after, lines 129-133; called for bm_entry at line ~186
findings.problem: _at_or_after returns the first benchmark row on or after the requested date with no bound on how far it may search. The prices archive starts 2015-01-01 but the indices archive starts 2015-11-09, so any event with an entry date in the first ten months of 2015 silently receives the 2015-11-09 index level as its ENTRY level. The resulting benchmark return spans a completely different window from the stock's.
findings.evidence:
prices range: 2015-01-01 to 2026-09-07
indices range: 2015-11-09 to 2026-09-07 ('Nifty 500': 2,671 rows, same span)
Nifty Total Market is worse: 1,210 rows against 2,084 for its peers over the same 2016-07-07 to 2026-09-07 span — an 874-session hole that _at_or_after will jump across without complaint.
findings.why_it_inflates: Currently dormant because both studies start in 2016, so this is a latent trap rather than an active error. But it is armed: any study extended back to 2015, or switched to Nifty Total Market as the benchmark (which the indices module explicitly recommends as 'the honest hurdle' for a multicap screen), would compare a stock's twelve months against an index window of arbitrary and undisclosed length, and would report the result with no indication that anything was wrong.
findings.fix: Have _at_or_after take a max_gap (a few sessions) and return None beyond it, so measure() marks the event unscored instead of fabricating a level. Add a startup assertion in measure() that the chosen benchmark's date coverage spans the full event range with no gap larger than a week, and fail loudly if it does not.
